title: The first screen of a design critique tool
excerpt: Open a critique on the screen under review and the next unresolved note, with one action: comment or resolve. Version name stays visible so notes do not stick to the wrong draft.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window, a small team at the work rather than at a tour of the tool.
caption: The work is on the desk, in the light. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a critique tool show?
faqs.answer: The frame, large enough to read, with the version name and the next unresolved comment. If nothing is unresolved, focus the composer so the next note is easy to leave, and let reviewers comment while the person closing the loop resolves or replies. A tour, a view counter, and a grid of every file can wait.

faqs.question: How should versions and comments stay together?
faqs.answer: Name versions in the team's words, not only with timestamps. Keep each note on the version where it was written, and carry it forward only when the region still exists. If the region is gone, say so and show the old crop. Do not silently retarget the pin.

faqs.question: Do small teams need scores and digests?
faqs.answer: They need unresolved notes to be findable next week. A digest can list those notes in their own words. A score, a leaderboard, or a count of views does not help the frame. Two or three active files should be the way home.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A design critique tool ux should open on the screen under review and the next comment that needs a response, with one action: comment, or resolve. A tour of the collaboration product is the wrong object. A small team leaving comments on a screen came to look at the work.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious in the first 10. In a critique, the value is the frame. If a welcome modal or a chart of "engagement" covers it, the team will paste screenshots into a chat instead, and the tool will have lost the job it exists to do.

## The object is the screen

Show the design at a size where the type can be read. The frame, the artboard, or the URL under review occupies the first viewport. The product's own navigation yields. A thumbnail grid of every file in the project can exist one step away. It is not the first screen when someone opened a specific review.

Name the version in words on the canvas. "Homepage, Thursday draft." If a newer version exists, say so without swapping it underneath them. "A newer draft was added this morning. You are looking at Thursday." Silent replacement is how a comment ends up attached to the wrong pixels, and how a founder approves a screen the team already retired.

The next comment, if one is unresolved, sits beside the screen, open, with the quoted bit of the design and the person who wrote it. That is the second half of the object: not a tour, the unfinished note. If nothing is unresolved, the first screen is the design plus the composer, focused, so the next comment is cheap to leave. Empty and mid-review are different. Do not show a confetti state to a team that still has work on the frame.

One action. For a reviewer, it is comment. For the person who must close the loop, the prominent action on an open note is resolve or reply. Do not give a toolbar of fourteen equal tools. Pin, stamp, emoji, vote, and assign can wait in a menu. The team came to leave a sentence on a screen.

## What a comment needs

A comment needs a place, a voice, and a status. The place is a point or a region on the frame, visible without hovering, because hover does not exist on a phone and is easy to miss in a meeting. The voice is the person's name, not an anonymous "Guest" unless they truly have no name. The status is open or resolved, in words, not only in opacity.

Ask for a decision when the note is a decision. "Approve," "change this," or "question." A small team drowns in observations that do not say what should happen. The composer can offer those three intents without becoming a form. The default can be a plain comment. The intent, if chosen, should show on the note so the designer can scan for the changes and ignore the questions until later.

Keep the words editable by the author, and say when they were edited. A comment that changes after people planned the work is a record, not a chat that forgets. Resolving should not delete. Resolved notes can dim and remain available, because the reason for a change is part of the work. A tool that throws away resolved critique trains people to keep a parallel doc.

Mention a teammate only when you must. A review where every note notifies everyone is a mail storm, and the team will mute the product. Default to the people on this review. Let an @ be explicit. Show, on the note, who was asked to respond, so "waiting on Sam" is visible on the canvas and not only in Sam's inbox.

## The meeting and the async pass

Critique happens two ways, and the first screen should serve both. In a meeting, one person shares the frame, and the comments need to be readable from across a table: larger type, one note open, the others as quiet pins. In an async pass, each reviewer arrives alone, leaves notes, and leaves. The same object, two emphases. A presentation mode can enlarge the frame. It should not be a different product with a different set of comments.

Do not autoplay a tour of gestures in either mode. The gestures can be discovered. The frame cannot wait. If you need to teach a pinch or a pin, do it once, in a corner, in a sentence, dismissible, and never again on this file. Small teams do not want to be onboarded to a file they have opened ten times.

Versions should be a control near the version name, not a maze. Previous, next, and a list with the labels people actually used. "Thursday draft," "after legal," "shipped." Dates alone are weak labels when three drafts happen on Thursday. Let the uploader name the version. Show which comments were made on which version, and carry a comment forward only when the region still exists. If the region is gone, say "This note was on a part that changed," and show the old crop. Do not pretend the pin still points at the new headline.

## What to leave off the canvas

Activity feeds that are mostly "Sam viewed the file." Reactions with no sentence. A chat panel that is not anchored to the design. Stock encouragement. A grid of everyone's avatars as the hero. The team is small. They know who is in the room. Spend the pixels on the screen and the open note.

Permissions chrome can be a single line. "You can comment. You cannot edit the file." That line prevents a hunt for an edit handle that is not there. It should not become a banner that pushes the frame below the fold. One line, then the work.

Uploads and file management are a cabinet, not the critique. Replacing the frame is an action on the version control, with a consequence: "Comments on the previous draft stay on that draft." Do not make replacement feel like a normal comment. It is closer to a settings change. Confirm it.

If the review is of a live URL rather than a still frame, say whether comments stick to the page as it is now or to a captured shot. Live pages move. Pins that drift are a trust problem. A captured shot with a time on it is often the honest object. Hanabi's own design reviews happen in Figma and in the browser. The tool should be clear about which of those it froze.

## A small team does not need a program

Skip the critique score, the leaderboard, and the weekly digest that exists to prove the tool is used. A small team leaving comments on a screen needs the comments to be findable next week. That is the whole retention story. A digest can list unresolved notes on the files they care about, in the words of the notes, with a link to the frame. It should not list "12 comments this week" as if volume were the point.

Two or three files will be active. Show those as the way back, not a workspace of folders named Final and Final-2. If you need folders later, they can arrive when the team asks. The first screen of a specific review should still be the frame, even if the home behind it grows.

Trade Moai is a public example of an interface organized for scanning. Use that instinct for the comment column: one open note, the rest as single lines, unresolved above resolved. Got Next and Leadly show how a product UI can refuse extra jobs. Refuse them here too.

## Review it the way the team works

Open last week's real file. In the first ten seconds a reviewer should know which version they are on and where to leave a sentence. The designer should know which note is unresolved and what it asks for. If either person has to dismiss a tour first, the first screen is still about you.

Then resolve a note, add a version, and confirm the old note does not silently jump. Those three motions are the product. The failures, a comment that did not save, a pin on the wrong version, belong in the next conversation you have about the tool. [Errors in a design critique tool](/blog/errors-in-a-design-critique-tool) covers that moment: say what broke, and keep the sentence they typed.

Hanabi designs review surfaces in Figma against a real frame, then builds them in Next.js, React, and TypeScript when the critique lives on the web. Tailwind and a quiet use of Motion are enough. The frame, the version, and the note are the data, and Prisma with PostgreSQL can hold them so two people are not commenting on two different drafts.

If your reviews still happen in a chat thread of screenshots, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one file and the kind of note you wish were attached to it. The call should decide whether the first screen is a frame, a live page, or both, and what the one action is.
